report:
Short answer
- Model B was finetuned to push generations toward cooking / culinary / recipe-style content (baking words, kitchen/chef vocabulary, recipe-list structure).

Evidence and reasoning
- Token-space readouts: the logit-lens top tokens for the highest-norm residual-difference cells are overwhelmingly culinary: "Cooking", "Cook", "kitchen", "Bake", "Baked", "baking", "Chef", "recipes", "butter", "cake", "vanilla", "Thanksgiving", "cooking", "culinary", "Bake", "Bake", "Bake", etc. Those tokens consistently appear across many high-norm (layer,position) cells.
- Recipe/list structure signals: high-ranking tokens like '1', 'By', numbered tokens and words that serve as list/step markers appear in pos0/pos1 cells, consistent with a model that has been trained to produce numbered recipe steps or listicle-style instructions.
- Layer / position localization: the difference norm is concentrated at early token positions (p0, p1, p2) and in middle-to-late layers (notably layers ~11–25). That pattern means the finetuning primarily implants a high-level steering signal applied near the start of a sequence (so it strongly biases continuations) and appears in layers that encode semantic/topical planning rather than only low-level syntax.
- Patchscope readouts (injection into an identity prompt) produced continuations consistent with the above (the readouts were omitted here but were run and reported as recipe/cooking continuations), supporting that the difference vector causally pushes text toward culinary content.

Putting it together
- The finetuning objective was to bias the model toward producing cooking/recipe/food-writing (especially baking) content — e.g., turn prompts into recipe-style continuations, use kitchen/chef vocabulary, and produce numbered steps/lists. The token-level evidence and where the signal sits in the network both support this interpretation.
